hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you mess up, is the voice inside you kinder or harsher than the one you’d use with a friend?
options: you’re not alone. this story starts with a very honest queen.
interesting. let’s see if a king and queen agree.
good. keep that. this story explains why it matters.

steps.line: In the Buddha’s time, King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika sat together one evening on the palace terrace.
The king asked her: “Mallika, is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?”

steps.q: He’s the king, and her husband. She answers him honestly. What does she do right after?
o: Turns the same question back on him
Begs his pardon for her answer
Asks him to take her to the Buddha
steps.why: “And you?” she asks, and he thinks, and admits the same. The story is kept twice in the Pali Canon, in the Udana and the Samyutta Nikaya.

steps.line: “No, great king,” she said. “No one is dearer to me than myself. And you?” He thought, and said: “No, Mallika. Not for me either.”
The king went to the Buddha and told him what they had said.

steps.q: What does the Buddha say about the queen’s answer?
o: She was selfish, and should take it back
Love for others should come first
She was right, and so is everyone
steps.why: He answers in verse: search every direction, and no one finds anyone dearer than themselves. He doesn’t scold; he widens it.

steps.line: The Buddha said: search every direction with your mind, and you’ll find no one dearer to anyone than themselves.
“So,” he said, “since each person holds themselves most dear, one who loves themselves should never harm another.”

steps.q: “Since each person holds themselves most dear, don’t harm others.” Which everyday rule does that sound most like?
o: Treat others as you’d want to be treated
Look after yourself before anyone else
Keep your distance and you won’t get hurt
steps.why: Many hear the Golden Rule in it. The Dhammapada says it too: all fear violence; seeing yourself in others, don’t harm (verses 129–130).

steps.q: Queen Mallika wasn’t born royal. Who was she before she married the king?
o: A nun who left the order
steps.why: The commentaries say she was a garland-maker’s daughter who became queen and one of the Buddha’s devoted followers. Her honesty here is famous.

steps.line: Today: the voice in the mirror after a long day. The Buddha’s reasoning starts right there. You’re dear to you. So is everyone else.
steps.label: today

steps.q: An old meditation guide lists who to wish well, in order. Who comes right after yourself?
steps.why: Buddhaghosa’s order: yourself, someone you respect, a dear friend, a stranger, then someone hostile. The hardest comes last, once the feeling is strong.

say: here’s what i love. the buddha didn’t scold the queen for loving herself. he took her honest answer and made it into kindness for everyone.

buddhists practice metta, loving-kindness: wanting good for someone the way a friend does. a famous old guide to meditation says to begin with yourself: may i be happy. you know from the inside that you want it, and so does everyone else.

steps.q: That old guide says to start loving-kindness with yourself, then widen it. How does this story explain why?
o: Your own wish to be happy shows you everyone’s
You must love yourself before anyone else
Others matter less until you’re well
steps.why: Buddhaghosa says you begin with yourself as the example: as I want to be happy, so does every being. Mallika’s honest answer makes the same move.

today.say: today, when you catch the harsh voice, say the friend’s sentence instead, quietly inside: may i be at ease. then widen it, the way metta does, to the next person you see: may you be at ease too.
options: good. you’re dear to you. that’s where it starts.
it will, at first. say it anyway. that counts.

sources: Mallika Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 3.8 (and Udana 5.1): King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika on the upper terrace of the palace; “Is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?” “There is no one, great king, dearer to me than myself. But is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?” “No, Mallika”; the king reports this to the Buddha, who replies in verse: having traversed all quarters with the mind, one finds none anywhere dearer than oneself; likewise each person holds themselves most dear; so one who loves themselves should not harm others (paraphrased from Bhikkhu Bodhi’s rendering).
Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga IX.8–10: loving-kindness is developed first toward oneself (“May I be happy”), with oneself as the example; this verse is cited there.
Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sutta Nipata 1.8): metta as a friend’s goodwill (background).

check: The predict and the “risky question” framing imply the king may have hoped to be named; the sutta does not say so (the commentary is said to). Confirm this is fair.
The Buddha’s verse is paraphrased in plain words; the lesson uses “themselves” for “oneself.”
Mallika’s appearance is invented for the paintings. The Buddha is shown in the traditional respectful way.
